newsitem.title: ITALY: MOTOR RACING-SENNA MANSLAUGHTER TRIAL ADJOURNED.
newsitem.headline: MOTOR RACING-SENNA MANSLAUGHTER TRIAL ADJOURNED.

text.p: Imola track director Federico Bendinelli was the only one of six defendants to turn up for the first day of the Ayrton Senna manslaughter trial on Thursday.

Formula One chief Frank Williams, Bendinelli plus four others have been accused of manslaughter after Brazilian three times world champion Senna died in the San Marino Grand Prix on May 1, 1994. All deny the charges
The trial was adjourned after three hours until February 28.

Bendinelli told reporters that no one should be held responsible for the freak accident in which Senna had been killed. The Brazilian died when his Williams car hurtled off the track and smashed into a concrete wall at around 220 kph.
The first session of the trial was held in a converted ballroom and dominated by demands from defence lawyers that much of the evidence against two of the accused should be ruled inadmissable.

Williams, Bendinelli, Imola circuit manager Giorgio Poggi, race director Roland Bruynseraede, Williams' technical director Patrick Head and designer Adrian Newey all face a maximum five years in jail if found guilty of the manslaughter charges.

Lawyers said much of the case built up over the last three years against Newey and Bruynseraede should be ignored because they had been warned they were under investigation only at the end of 1996 when prosecutors demanded their trial.
"This is a scandal. It should not happen in a civilised country," Newey's lawyer Luigi Stortoni told the court.
The presiding judge, 35-year old Antonio Costanzo, will rule on the request at the next sitting.

"The death was due exclusively to the fact that part of the suspension block on one of the wheels snapped off and broke through (Senna's) visor to hit his forehead. It was like a bullet," Bendinelli told reporters on Thursday.
"If it was not for this bizarre blow, Senna would have been able to walk away from the accident."

Chief public prosecutor Maurizio Passarini believes Senna lost control of his car because poor welding on the steering column snapped. He has also accused racing officials of allowing the Grand Prix to take place on a dangerous track.
"We are absolutely convinced the car was in good order. The steering column broke after and not before the crash," said Oreste Dominioni, one of Williams' team of lawyers.
He told reporters that Williams would take part in the trial as much as possible. "He will probably be at the hearing in March when the prosecution lays out its case," Dominioni said.
Passarini is due to open the prosecution on March 5 and the first witnesses are due to be heard from March 11.

Among those being called to testify, the court heard on Thursday, is current Formula One world champion Damon Hill, who took over from Senna in the Williams team in 1994, and left the squad at the end of last season.
The trial is likely to last for several months, with only two sessions a week scheduled for the makeshift courtroom, which has been set up just two km from the Imola race track where Senna died.
A lawyer representing Senna's family was in court and said he would follow the case as an observor. "The family is interested but is not taking sides," Giovanni Carcaterra said.
The 1994 race was marred by tragedy. Besides Senna, Austrian driver Roland Ratzenerger also died in a high-speed smash. Their deaths were the first in Formula One for 12 years.
"It seems there was a curse on the 1994 Grand Prix," Bendinelli said. (c) Reuters Limited 1997
